opening.headline: As we increase the number of tools, we address the issue of models selecting inappropriate tools by designing tools with their names, descriptions, and response designs.
body: It worked well when the agent had four tools, but as we added functionality and increased the number of tools to nearly forty, it started calling the wrong tools. Before changing the model, there's something we should first consider: the model knows about tools only through textual information such as their names, descriptions, and parameter definitions.

In this course, we view tools not as interfaces used by humans via APIs, but as interfaces readable by models. We examine in sequence the criteria for naming and describing tools, methods for keeping responses lightweight, and the role of error messages. Then, we learn through examples how to decide among three approaches—integrating, separating, or modifying descriptions—of tools.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: The tool name, description, and response design can explain their impact on the model's tool selection accuracy.
When tool selection errors increase, it becomes possible to determine the appropriate approach among integration, separation, and explanation improvements.

screens.title: After expanding the options, ends up selecting the wrong tool.
screens.lead: First, read the scene that actually occurs within an agent where tools have been expanded. While reading, consider what might be the cause of the issue.

visual.alt: A side-by-side comparison of the tool list and call logs when there are 4 tools versus when there are 40 tools.
labels: Request: Find payment log for customer 9182 → search_logs(customer_id=9182)

paragraphs: Initially, the internal agent had only four tools. At that time, it handled requests well. However, as more functionalities were added and the number of tools grew to nearly forty, the agent began calling the wrong tools.

Let's consider the user's request: "Find me the logs related to customer 9182 having made three payments." Instead of calling an agent that retrieves only logs matching the specified condition, the agent was called to return all logs. As a result, thousands of log lines filled the context, yet the actual answer needed was not provided.

Tool definitions are included in the model's context every time a request is sent. When connecting servers such as GitHub, Slack, Sentry, Grafana, and Splunk, it can result in consuming approximately 55,000 tokens solely through definitions. Additionally, Claude explains that tool selection accuracy decreases when the number of available tools exceeds 30 to 50.

This issue is often not due to a lack of model capability, but rather because the tool's name, description, and response presented an unkind interface to the model. This course addresses how to fix such an interface.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: When the number of tools increases to forty, the cost of context retention due to tool definition and the cost of context filling caused by a delayed response from an incorrect tool are two distinct issues. By the end of the lesson, these two problems can be clearly differentiated and explained.

screens.outro: Having confirmed the scope of the issue, let me first recall how we should determine the name and description.

screens.title: Preview: Criteria for name and description
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thoughts are displayed. There is no step to enter or submit an answer; instead, first think about it mentally, then click to view.

items.prompt: What criteria are you using to define tool names and descriptions?
items.answer: In many cases, the creator assigns intuitive, easy-to-understand names. However, the model does not understand the creator's mental context. The only basis the model has for understanding a tool is the text in its name and description. Therefore, the criterion becomes not "whether the creator can understand it," but "whether a model encountering it for the first time can select it without confusion."

items.prompt: Can a newly joined colleague understand what tasks they're performing just by seeing the tool name?
items.answer: If a colleague cannot figure out what something is just from its name, then the model also cannot. Names like "search" or "run" do not indicate what they do or where they are located. Anthropic recommends writing tool descriptions as if explaining them to a new team member. This metaphor becomes the standard for the entire course.

items.prompt: If the parameter name is only "user", should we put in the name or the ID?
items.answer: The model must make an assumption. If the assumption is wrong, it results in a call with incorrect parameters. The documentation advises using clear names such as user_id instead of ambiguous terms like user. A simple change of one name reduces call errors.

items.prompt: If there are three similar tools available, on what basis will the model choose one?
items.answer: The difference is merely in name and description. When the difference is unclear, selection becomes unclear. When tools overlap or purposes are ambiguous, the model becomes confused about which tool to use—this is the first issue that arises when increasing the number of tools.

screens.outro: I will check each item one by one against the criteria I have recalled.

screens.title: Tools are a contract between deterministic code and nondeterministic agents
screens.lead: We examine the tool call flow step by step. You can proceed to the next step by selecting the right arrow, and navigate back to the previous step using the left arrow.

visual.alt: A four-step flow diagram involving tool definition transmission between application and model, tool call return, function execution, and result return.
labels: The model sees only the definition text.

steps.title: From the perspective of a contract
steps.body: Traditional software is a contract between deterministic systems. A function call like getWeather("NYC") returns the same result every time it is invoked. Tools represent a new kind of contract between deterministic code and agents that can behave differently under the same conditions.

steps.title: Step 1: Deliver the definition
steps.body: Send a list of tools with the request. Each tool is defined by name, description, and parameter schema. Both OpenAI and Gemini's function calling documentation describe the same structure, allowing the schema to indicate required parameters. The model determines which tool to use based solely on this text.

steps.title: Step 2: The model makes the request.
steps.body: The model returns a request to call a certain function with certain arguments if it deems it necessary. For the same query, an agent might call a weather tool, answer based on knowledge, or retrieve location information. The model may misuse tools if it does not understand how to use them.

steps.title: Step 3: The application is executed
steps.body: The side that actually executes the function is not the model but the application. The model only requests the call, and the developer's code receives the arguments and invokes the function.

steps.title: Step 4: Return the result
steps.body: The execution result is returned to the model along with the call ID as tool call output. The model reads this result and generates the final response. The size and structure of the result directly determine the size and quality of the next context.

steps.title: Therefore, the design target changes.
steps.body: You should not create tools that replicate functions and APIs used by developers and other systems. Instead, you must design interfaces that agents can read and write. Often, tools that are convenient for agents are also intuitive for humans to understand.

screens.outro: Since we have confirmed that the model reads only definition text, let's compare a poor definition with a good one for the same functionality.

screens.title: The same functionality, bad definition and good definition
screens.lead: Compare the differences in defining the same functionality by alternately selecting between two states. While reading, keep in mind that the model sees only this text.

states.label: bad definition
states.body:
The name is `search`, the description is "searches", and the parameters are `user` and `query`.

```json
{"name": "search", "description": "searches", "parameters": {"user": "string", "query": "string"}}
```

It is not clear what is being searched for or where. It does not specify whether this is for a project or a task, nor does it indicate how many results are expected. It is unclear whether `user` refers to a name or an ID, so the model must infer this. Additionally, it does not distinguish between similar tools that may exist, making it unclear which one should be used.

states.label: good definition
states.body:
The name is `asana_search`, the description clarifies the scope and use case of the tool, and the parameters are specified as `user_id` to eliminate ambiguity.

```json
{"name": "asana_search", "description": "Searches for projects and tasks in Asana using keywords. Returns a maximum of 10 results.", "parameters": {"user_id": "string (the ID of the assignee)", "query": "string (the search keyword)"}}
```

The tool description is written as one would explain it to a new team member. It extracts contextual meaning—such as the definitions of technical terms, query formats, and relationships between resources—into clear sentences. By appending service prefixes like `asana_search`, `jira_search` or resource prefixes like `asana_projects_search`, the boundaries between overlapping tools become clearer. Since the effectiveness of prefix-based versus suffix-based naming varies depending on the model, the documentation recommends that users determine the most appropriate approach based on their own evaluation.

screens.outro: If the definition has improved, now let's examine the response returned by the tool from the same perspective.

screens.title: Response Design: Size, Identifier, Error Messages
screens.lead: Select each tab to explore three key topics you should pay attention to in the tool response.

tabs.label: response size
tabs.body:
The model reads the content returned by the tool token by token. `list_contacts`, which returns the entire contact list, causes the tool to read through all entries in order to find a single person. When searching for a name in a contact list, it's similar to jumping directly to the relevant page rather than reading from the first to the last. A tool like `search_contacts`, which finds only what's needed, is preferable.

If the tool can generate a large context, page splitting, range selection, filtering, and truncation are provided with reasonable default settings. Claude Code limits tool responses to a default of 25,000 tokens.

tabs.label: Identifier and Format
tabs.body:
Instead of returning low-level technical values such as `uuid`, `256px_image_url`, and `mime_type`, it returns values used for judgment such as `name`, `image_url`, and `file_type`. The document explains that simply renaming arbitrary alphanumeric IDs to meaningful names reduced hallucinations and improved search accuracy.

In cases where an ID is needed for subsequent calls, the model can select between `response_format` and `concise` or `detailed` via the `response_format` parameter. In the Slack example provided in the document, the `concise` response used approximately one-third of the tokens of `detailed`. The format of the response—whether in XML, JSON, or Markdown—can affect performance and is therefore specified as part of the evaluation.

tabs.label: Errors and truncated responses
tabs.body:
Opaque errors or stack traces like `invalid input` do not indicate what the model should fix. Error messages that specify what went wrong and what the correct input should look like prompt the model to self-correct and retry.  

When truncating responses, we also include guidance. For example, stating "Results were too numerous; only a subset is returned. Apply a date filter and search again" encourages the model to adopt more efficient strategies. Guidance that prompts multiple small, specific searches is better than a single broad search.

screens.outro: Since the response has been refined, let's examine how to adjust the number of tools and boundaries.

screens.title: Tool integration, tool search, programmatic invocation
screens.lead: Select items to expand and learn step by step how to reduce the number of tools and overhead. You can also expand multiple items simultaneously for comparison.

items.title: Unified: Merge frequently occurring calls into one
items.body: Instead of using three tools—`list_users`, `list_events`, and `create_event`—you can use just one scheduler, `schedule_event`. Instead of using `get_customer_by_id`, `list_transactions`, and `list_notes`, you can aggregate recent relevant information into a single `get_customer_context`, and instead of using `read_logs`, you can simply provide relevant links via `search_logs`. Intermediate results are processed within the tool and do not occupy context.

items.title: The limitations of integration: the objective must be clear
items.body: Integration is effective when each tool has a clear and distinct purpose. Forcing tools with different purposes into a single context leads to longer, more complex explanations and entangled parameters, ultimately making things more ambiguous. In such cases, separate by purpose and establish boundaries using service and resource prefixes. When many tools overlap or have ambiguous purposes, the model finds it difficult to adopt efficient strategies.

items.title: Tool search: Load only the required definitions
items.body: Instead of loading all tool definitions, this approach has the model search for and retrieve only the necessary tools. According to the Claude documentation, a typical multi-server setup consumes only about 55,000 tokens for definitions, and tool search reduces this by over 85%, retrieving only 3 to 5 tools per request. This method also helps maintain selection accuracy when tools exceed 30 to 50. OpenAI recommends using tool search when there are many functions or large schemas, and advises deferring the use of rarely used tools.

items.title: Programming-style tool invocation: repeat queries via code
items.body: When the same query needs to be repeated, such as checking the budget for 20 employees, instead of having the model make and receive 50 calls, it calls the tool within the code execution environment using a loop. Intermediate results do not enter the model's context; only the filtered results are returned to the model. This method reduces both the number of calls and the token count.

screens.outro: Since there are multiple methods, this proceeds with case studies to illustrate which method to use based on symptoms.

screens.title: Case Explanation: Agent with Increased Tool Selection Errors
screens.lead: The instructor breaks down the process of analyzing symptoms in an agent with 38 tools step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed step by step.

steps.title: Check for symptoms
steps.body: The agent with 38 tools alternately invokes `search` and `find_items` for the same request. When reviewing the logs, the context becomes fully saturated at once. First, acknowledge that the symptoms are not a single issue but multiple ones, and then determine where to begin addressing them.

steps.title: Step 1: Classify the symptoms
steps.body: Parse the call records and categorize them into three types: mistaken tool selection due to similar names, parameter errors caused by ambiguous parameters such as `user`, and context overload resulting from returning the full list. If there are many duplicate calls in the call records, suspect pagination issues; if there are many parameter errors, suspect documentation issues.

steps.title: Step 2: Integrate
steps.body: Combines three consecutive queries into one `get_customer_context`. `read_logs` is replaced with `search_logs`, which returns only the relevant rows. The tool becomes lighter, and intermediate results no longer accumulate in the context.

steps.title: Step 3: Improve the explanation
steps.body: This explains when to use and when not to use two confusing search tools. Replace `user` with `user_id`. When configuration is reasonable and parameter errors recur, such minor documentation updates have led to significant improvements.

steps.title: Step 4: Create a name space
steps.body: Appends a service prefix to tools of the same type to establish boundaries. For example, dividing `asana_search` and `jira_search` allows the model to distinguish the target system simply by examining the name. Determine which approach is better based on your own evaluation.

steps.title: Step 5: Solve the remaining problems
steps.body: Even after integration and improved explanations, having dozens of tools makes the definition itself problematic. When tool search retrieves only the necessary definitions, both context and selection accuracy are preserved. Finally, we create a realistic evaluation task that requires multiple tool calls to be completed, to verify whether accuracy, number of calls, tokens, and error rates have improved.

screens.outro: Let's take one case as an example; we will generalize by using a reference table to determine which treatment is appropriate based on symptoms.

screens.title: Integration, separation, and improvement of explanations: criteria for deciding what to do
screens.lead: The following table summarizes three prescribing scenarios, the signals that appear, and points to watch for. Read it row by row and connect the entries with the previous examples.

data.caption: Prescription comparison for tool selection errors
rows: When the call order is nearly fixed and intermediate results only occupy context.
The same combination of calls is repeated, and the intermediate results are excessively long and unrelated to the final answer.
Tools are grouped only when their purposes are clearly defined and distinct. Forcing grouping of tools with different purposes leads to ambiguity.
When a single tool is used to explain different purposes, leading to longer descriptions and intertwined parameters.
The description is lengthy, exhibits entirely different behaviors depending on the argument combination, and the model misinterprets the arguments.
Establishes boundaries using service and resource prefixes. If the number of split tools becomes excessively large, consider tool search as well.
The tool configuration is reasonable, but repeated argument errors and invalid queries occur.
Ambiguous parameter names, repeated same-argument errors, confusion among similar tools
Write it as if explaining to a new team member. There are cases where minor wording adjustments have led to significant improvements, so evaluate the effectiveness accordingly.
When tool definitions exceed dozens, and context is rapidly inferred solely from definitions.
The tool count exceeds 30 to 50, and the definition token size grows significantly per request.
Since only 3 to 5 items are needed, the tool name and description must be clearly searchable.
data.notes: Any prescription is compared before and after improvement using the same evaluation task. Create realistic tasks requiring multiple tool calls and examine accuracy, number of calls, tokens, and error count together.

screens.outro: Having established the standards, I will now organize the process from symptoms to prescription in a sequential flow.

screens.title: From symptoms to prescription: organizing the decision flow
screens.lead: This summarizes the previous content in the flow of symptoms, causes, and solutions.

paragraphs: If the wrong tool is chosen, the cause is generally due to ambiguous or overlapping names and descriptions. The solution is to improve descriptions, manage naming spaces, and integrate systems. Names should be distinct, descriptions should be clear as if explaining to a new team member, and parameters should be defined without ambiguity.

If the context fills quickly, the cause is likely due to large tool responses. The remedy involves filtering, pagination, and truncation, with a note guiding the model to apply the following strategy to the truncated response. When errors occur, it informs the model of what went wrong and provides the correct format, enabling the model to correct itself autonomously.
If there are too many tool definitions, retrieve only the necessary ones via tool search. If there are many repeated queries, return only the results via programmed tool calls to the model.

The foundation of all these judgments is the same perspective. Tools are interfaces for models. Instead of wrapping developer APIs directly, start by creating a small number of clear tools that respect the agent's limited context.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Before blaming the model for degraded performance as tools increase, first verify the tool's name, description, and response. Select prescriptions based on symptoms and confirm effectiveness through the same evaluation process.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: The tool only returns an "invalid input" error, causing the model to repeatedly make the same incorrect call. What is the most appropriate improvement?
options: Converts error codes into numbers to make them shorter and more consistent.
Remove the retry limit so the model continuously attempts.
The error message states what is wrong and what the correct format should look like.
If an error occurs, remove the tool from the list and select another tool.
checks.explain: If the model is given incorrect error messages or proper formatting, it can self-correct and re-call accordingly. Errors are also part of the interface the model reads.

wrong.0: A model cannot know what needs to be fixed based solely on numeric codes.
wrong.1: Trying repeatedly without revealing the cause will result in the same failures recurring.
wrong.3: The problem is not a tool but an error message. Removing the tool results in losing only functionality.

checks.intro: Pair up the situation with the prescription. The result is not recorded.
checks.q: Match the most appropriate prescription to the following scenario.
left: Three queries are always called consecutively and only hold context for intermediate results.
One tool involves explanations that are long and complex due to multiple, distinct purposes.
The tool configuration is reasonable, but repeated errors occur with ambiguous parameters such as user.
The tool definitions themselves number in the dozens, enabling rapid context establishment through mere definition.
right: Tool search that retrieves only 3~5 necessary definitions

Refinement of descriptions and parameter names  
Improvement of documentation
Separation by purpose and boundary establishment using service and resource prefixes
A unified tool that gathers multiple queries at once
checks.explain: If the call order is fixed, integrate; if objectives are mixed, separate; if the structure matches but parameter errors recur, improve the explanation; if the issue lies in the definition itself, search for tools.

glossary.def: This is a call request that provides the tool definition and returns a function name and arguments. The actual execution is performed by the application.
This is a way, similar to asana_search, where a prefix is appended to indicate the boundary of services or resources containing the tool.
This is a parameter that allows the model to uniformly select the level of detail for tool responses, either concise or detailed.
This is a feature that retrieves and loads only the required tools upon search, rather than pre-loading all tool definitions.
This approach involves repeatedly calling the tool within the code execution environment, filtering the results, and returning only the filtered results to the model.

misconceptions.fact: The more similar or overlapping tools there are, the more choices become ambiguous, and definitions end up taking precedence over context. A small number of tools with clear purposes is preferable.

misconceptions.myth: Wrapping the API endpoint directly in a tool is sufficient.
misconceptions.fact: Agents have limited contexts, so designing them to return a full list results in waste. They should be designed instead as search or integration tools tailored to their specific behaviors.

misconceptions.myth: Error messages should only be viewed by developers.
misconceptions.fact: The model reads error messages and retries itself. Error messages that indicate the correct format improve performance.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The tool is an interface for the model, therefore designed like a document that agents can read, rather than a developer-facing API.
Names should be distinct, descriptions should be given to new team members as if explaining to them, and parameters should be defined clearly without ambiguity.
The response returns only meaningful values and provides error messages that explain how to fix the issue.
Overlapping tools are consolidated, but if there are still many, only the necessary definitions are loaded via tool search.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Which of my agent's tools should be integrated or renamed?
